newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Ike Turner Jr. battles obscurity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Ike Turner Jr. battles obscurity.

text.p: He looks, plays and sounds like his father, but after more than a decade trying to emulate the success of Ike Turner and stepmother Tina, he still battles obscurity.

"You could be Bill Clinton's son but you still have to be good at what you do. Having a name just really makes it that much harder ... the expectations of people," Ike Turner Jr. said, letting his words trail off with a shrug of his shoulders. Like President Clinton's brother Roger, Turner has failed to set the music world on fire, playing other people's songs to half-empty cabaret halls.
"All I really need is one hit record," he said. "I've been at it for quite a while."

Turner's stepmother is still a top star and his father is trying to rebuild his career after serving a jail term for selling drugs. The young Turner seems to have been getting ready for fame all his life. At age 5, he started playing the drums before shifting to the piano because his stepmother found the drums too loud. By 13, he took to the road, working as a sound engineer on a tour with Ike & Tina Turner and music legends Frank Zappa, Led Zeppelin and Billy Preston. In 1982 he started "Ike Turner Jr. and The Second Generation."
Now 15 years later, at the age of 37, he has put together a new lineup of Second Generation in the hope it will finally take him to the top.
SAYS HE CAN WAIT FOR FAME

"I'm not in a rush," Turner said. "I don't make a whole lot of money when I'm on the road but we get the same treatment as Tina or Michael Jackson, the same thing. As long as I'm making a living and I'm able to build this Second Generation thing."

Turner unveiled his latest lineup, which includes his brother Ronnie on bass guitar and cousin Jackie on vocals, at Saint Mark's, a club in Venice Beach, California. The show started late one night recently as the band and the audience waited for Turner's famous father to arrive to play a tune or two with his sons.
But Ike Sr. never did not show up. When the band finally took the stage, it was as though the audience was back in 1966 watching the Ike and Tina Turner Revue, Ikettes and all.

The Second Generation offers a pulsing beat, a female lead vocalist, backup singers and 1960s-style choreographed dance moves. Not only did they look like the Ike & Tina Revue but the band played the elders' best-known songs, "River Deep, Mountain High" and "Proud Mary."

The rest of the set, which lasted barely an hour, included Sly Stone and Marvin Gaye songs and The Beatles' song "Get Back." Turner, playing on keyboard, performed three songs he wrote himself, including one entitled "I Can't Stand It."
He said he planned to tour with the band for the next two years, hoping a break will come.

"Pyramid Power" is the strangely mystical way Turner describes the way he works. "Pyramid power is a unit. We all work as a unit with me at the top. Definitely, that's where all the energy comes from."

Turner, who recently moved to Redondo Beach, California, from St. Louis, was reluctant to talk much about life with Ike and Tina, whose stormy 18-year marriage ended in the summer of 1976. Tina Turner detailed the beatings and abuse she endured at the hands of her bandleader husband in her 1986 autobiography, "I, Tina." It was followed by the biographical 1993 film "What's Love Got to Do With It."

Ike Sr. was sentenced to 18 months in jail in 1991 for selling cocaine and is now trying to resurrect his career with a new band. Ike Jr. does not see much of either his father or his stepmother these days. He says he has not seen Tina in almost five years.
But, asked if he had any regrets about his life, he said: "I probably wouldn't have started travelling and hanging around my father and all them at such a young age."
